title: Counters and calendars
description:
Write the time conversions of lesson 2.03:

```cpp
std::int64_t countsToMicroseconds(std::int64_t counts, std::int64_t frequency);
std::int64_t fileTimeToUnixMs(std::uint64_t fileTime);     // 100 ns units since 1601-01-01 UTC
std::uint64_t unixMsToFileTime(std::int64_t unixMs);
std::string formatUtc(std::uint64_t fileTime);             // "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS"
```

- `countsToMicroseconds` must not overflow for large counts (such as a counter of `10 000 000` per second after 30 days of uptime): split the counts into whole seconds and the remainder before multiplying. Round down.
- Between 1601 and 1970 there are `11 644 473 600` seconds. `fileTimeToUnixMs` rounds down to the millisecond (towards minus infinity for times before 1970).
- `formatUtc` converts the file time to a date and time in the Gregorian calendar (leap years: divisible by 4, except centuries, except every 400 years). Times are never before 1601.
hints: For the date, first turn the file time into whole days and seconds within the day; then convert days to a year, month and day. Treating March as the first month of the year puts the leap day at the end, which makes the arithmetic much simpler.

A plain loop works too, and is fast enough here: starting from 1601, subtract 365 or 366 days for each whole year while the days left are at least a year, then do the same with the month lengths of that year (February has 29 days in a leap year).
